latin: nam idem tunc episcopum Romanum, agnoscentem iam prophetias Montani Priscae Maximillae et ex ea agnitione pacem ecclesiis Asiae et Phrygiae inferentem, falsa de ipsis prophetis et ecclesiis eorum adseuerando et praecessorum eius auctoritates defendendo coegit et litteras pacis reuocare iam emissas et a proposito recipiendorum charismatum concessare. ita duo negotia diaboli Praxeas Romae procurauit: prophetiam expulit et haeresim intulit, paracletum fugauit et patrem crucifixit.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: For after the Bishop of Rome had acknowledged the prophetic gifts of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and, in consequence of the acknowledgment, had bestowed his peace on the churches of Asia and Phrygia, he, by importunately urging false accusations against the prophets themselves and their churches, and insisting on the authority of the bishop's predecessors in the see, compelled him to recall the pacific letter which he had issued, as well as to desist from his purpose of acknowledging the said gifts. By this Praxeas did a twofold service for the devil at Rome: he drove away prophecy, and he brought in heresy; he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.
page: CSEL 47 p. 228 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Tertullian's own account of Praxeas, who brought the heresy from Asia to Rome; he charges him with having 'crucified the Father'.
use: context: shows what the controversy was about (Patripassianism as Tertullian reports it), not a doctrinal statement.
limits: Polemical, ad hominem; a report of an opponent's position, not Tertullian's own doctrine. Do not present 'crucified the Father' as neutral history.

latin: 2. Itaque post tempus pater natus et pater passus, ipse deus dominus omnipotens, Iesus Christus praedicatur. nos uero et semper et nunc magis.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: In the course of time, then, the Father forsooth was born, and the Father suffered, God Himself, the Lord Almighty, whom in their preaching they declare to be Jesus Christ. We, however, as we indeed always have done (and more especially since we have been better instructed by the Paraclete, who leads men indeed into all truth),
page: CSEL 47 p. 228-229 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: States the Patripassian formula that Tertullian rejects (Father born and suffered) and sets his own rule of faith against it.
use: objection: quote this as the view Tertullian is refuting, then set chapter 2's rule of faith against it.
limits: The 'pater natus / pater passus' formula is Tertullian's summary of the Patripassian view; this treatise does not show it as a verbatim Praxean sentence. The Latin of 'nos uero' runs on in the next item.

latin: nos uero et semper et nunc magis. ut instructiores per paracletum, deductorem scilicet omnis ueritatis, unicum quidem deum credimus, sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oikonomiam dicimus, ut unici dei sit et filius, sermo ipsius, qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt et sine quo factum est nihil.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: believe that there is one only God, but under the following dispensation, or οἰκονομία, as it is called, that this one only God has also a Son, His Word, who proceeded from Himself, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.
page: CSEL 47 p. 229 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Son is the Word of the one God, who 'proceeded from' the Father (processerit), through whom all things were made (Jn 1:3).
use: supports Trinitarian reading: the Son is a Son and Word of the one God; the Word 'proceeds' (procession, not separate deity).
limits: Does not give the Son's eternity or timing; 'processerit' is not 'generatus'. Opponents (Arian, Sabellian) read the 'proceeded' language as a creature's origin. The chapter 2 rule is a rule of faith, not a definition of Nicene terms.

latin: quasi non sic quoque unus sit omnia, dum ex uno omnia, per substantiae scilicet unitatem, et nihilominus custodiatur oikonomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens patrem et filium et spiritum
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: as if in this way also one were not All, in that All are of One, by unity (that is) of substance; while the mystery of the dispensation is still guarded, which distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons— the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost:
page: CSEL 47 p. 229 (Latin); first attested 'trinitatem' in this treatise; ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The one substance (substantiae unitas) is the basis of the unity; the economy distributes that one unity into a Trinity of three persons. This is the first occurrence of trinitatem in Adv. Prax. (none in ch. 1).
use: supports Trinitarian reading: 'per substantiae unitatem' ties the three to one substance; 'trinitas' is used as Tertullian's own term for the three persons.
limits: The word 'trinitas' is used here of the economy, not defined. This is the first use within Adv. Prax., not an established first use in Tertullian's corpus (not checked). 'Persons' in the ANF is the translator's word; the Latin of this sentence has only 'tres'.

latin: tres dirigens patrem et filium et spiritum, tres autem non statu, sed gradu. nec substantia, sed forma, nec potestate, sed specie, unius autem substantiae et unius status et unius potestatis, quia unus deus, ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti deputantur.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power, inasmuch as He is one God, from whom these degrees and forms and aspects are reckoned, under the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
page: CSEL 47 p. 229-230 (Latin); the 'tres ... unius substantiae' sentence is on p. 230; ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The three are 'tres', but not three in status, substance or power: they are three gradus, formae, species of one substance, status and potestas, from the one God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: 'unius substantiae' explicitly; the three are one substance and one power. This is the passage on 'substantia / status / gradus / forma / species' the brief asks about.
limits: Arians and Subordinationists cite 'non statu sed gradu' and 'gradus' as proof of rank or unequal degree. Tertullian's terms are not the Nicene vocabulary. 'Gradus' in Adv. Prax. is a term of economy and order, not a verdict on equality here.

latin: Simplices enim quique, ne dixerim imprudentes et idiotae, quae maior semper credentium pars est, quoniam et ipsa regula fidei a pluribus diis saeculi ad unicum et verum deum transfert, non intellegentes unicum quidem sed cum sua oikonomia esse credendum, expauescunt, quod oikonomiam numerum et dispositionem trinitatis diuisionem praesumunt unitatis,
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: The simple, indeed, (I will not call them unwise and unlearned,) who always constitute the majority of believers, are startled at the dispensation (of the Three in One), on the ground that their very rule of faith withdraws them from the world's plurality of gods to the one only true God; not understanding that, although He is the one only God, He must yet be believed in with His own οἰκονομία. The numerical order and distribution of the Trinity they assume to be a division of the Unity;
page: CSEL 47 p. 230 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Simple believers fear that the 'dispensation' (number and order of the Trinity) divides the Unity; Tertullian says the one God must be believed with his economy.
use: answer to objection: the 'tres dii / division of unity' charge; Tertullian says the economy does not divide the one God.
limits: This is Tertullian's answer to his opponents' objection; it is not a precise statement of later Trinitarian doctrine. The 'oikonomia' answer needs the rest of the work.

latin: 'monarchiam', inquiunt, 'tenemus,' et ita sonum ipsum uocaliter exprimunt etiam Latini et tam opifice, ut putes illos tam bene intellegere monarchiam quam enuntiant. [sed monarchiam sonare student Latini, oikonomiam intellegere nolunt etiam Graeci.] at ego, si quid utriusque linguae praecerpsi, monarchiam nihil aliud significare scio quam singulare et unicum imperium; non tamen praescribere monarchiam ideo, quia unius sit, eum, cuius sit, aut filium non habere aut ipsum se sibi filium fecisse aut monarchiam suam non per quos uelit administrare.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: We, say they, maintain the Monarchy (or, sole government of God). And so, as far as the sound goes, do even Latins (and ignorant ones too) pronounce the word in such a way that you would suppose their understanding of the μοναρχία ( or Monarchy) was as complete as their pronunciation of the term. Well, then Latins take pains to pronounce the μοναρχία (or Monarchy), while Greeks actually refuse to understand the οἰκονομία, or Dispensation (of the Three in One). As for myself, however, if I have gleaned any knowledge of either language, I am sure that μοναρχία (or Monarchy) has no other meaning than single and individual rule; but for all that, this monarchy does not, because it is the government of one, preclude him whose government it is, either from having a son, or from having made himself actually a son to himself, or from ministering his own monarchy by whatever agents he will.
page: CSEL 47 p. 230-231 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Tertullian defines monarchia as single and individual rule, which does not exclude a Son or delegated agents. This is his answer to the monarchian charge.
use: answer to objection (monarchian 'monarchia' argument); the key definition of monarchia in the treatise.
limits: The bracketed Latin sentence ('sed monarchiam sonare student... etiam Graeci') is secluded by Kroymann (apparatus: 'etiam Graeci seclusi'); ANF translates it as if authentic. Quote the ANF with that caveat.

latin: si uero et filius fuerit ei, cuius monarchia sit, non statim diuidi eam et monarchiam esse desinere, si particeps eius adsumatur et filius, sed proinde illius esse principaliter, a quo communicatur in filium, et dum illius est, proinde monarchiam esse, quae a duobus tam unitis continetur.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: If, moreover, there be a son belonging to him whose monarchy it is, it does not immediately become divided and cease to be a monarchy, if the son also be taken as a sharer in it; but it is as to its origin equally his, by whom it is communicated to the son; and being his, it is quite as much a monarchy (or sole empire), since it is held together by two who are so inseparable.
page: CSEL 47 p. 231 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: A Son who shares the monarchy does not divide it; it is the Father's in origin and communicated to the Son, held together by two inseparable.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: shared rule without division; the 'communicatur in filium' language gives the Son a share of the one substance and rule.
limits: 'Principaliter' (the Father is the principal origin) is what Arians cite for the Father's priority. Kroymann adopts Engelbrecht's 'unitis' against the manuscripts' 'unicis' (apparatus: 'unitis Eng: unicis PMF').

latin: igitur si et monarchia diuina per tot legiones et exercitus angelorum administratur, sicut scriptum est: milies centies centena milia adsistebant ei, et milies centena milia apparebant ei, nec ideo unius esse desiit, ut desinat monarchia esse, quia per tanta milia uirtutum procuratur:
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: Therefore, inasmuch as the Divine Monarchy also is administered by so many legions and hosts of angels, according as it is written, Thousand thousands ministered unto Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before Him; Daniel 7:10 and since it has not from this circumstance ceased to be the rule of one (so as no longer to be a monarchy), because it is administered by so many thousands of powers;
page: CSEL 47 p. 231 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The divine monarchy is run through many angels without ceasing to be one rule; the same goes for Son and Spirit.
use: answer to objection: the monarchy is not broken by delegated agents (angels as the analogy for the Son and Spirit).
limits: Tertullian separates the Son and Spirit from the angels (see next item), so the angel analogy is an analogy of administration only; it does not make the Son a creature.

ref: chapter 3 (Kroymann and ANF division; 'secundum et tertium' = second and third place)
latin: quale est, ut deus diuisionem et dispersionem pati uideatur in filio et in spiritu sancto, secundum et tertium sortitis locum, tam consortibus substantiae patris, quas non patitur in tot angelorum numero, et quidem tam <alienorum> a substantia patris?
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: how comes it to pass that God should be thought to suffer division and severance in the Son and in the Holy Ghost, who have the second and the third places assigned to them, and who are so closely joined with the Father in His substance, when He suffers no such (division and severance) in the multitude of so many angels?
page: CSEL 47 p. 231 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Son and Spirit have the second and third places, yet are 'consortes' of the Father's substance, unlike the angels; the 'second' and 'third' is a place in order, not a separate substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son and Spirit 'consortes substantiae patris'); also the ANF 'second and third places' gloss on secundum/tertium.
limits: The phrase '<alienorum>' (angels 'so alien from the substance of the Father') is an editorial supplement by Gelenius (apparatus: 'tam <(alienorum)> Gel'); the ANF omits that clause, so do not cite the ANF as a full rendering. 'Secundum' here is an ordinal of place: do not read it as subordinate rank without the context.

latin: Ceterum qui filium non aliunde deduco, sed de substantia patris, nihil facientem sine patris uoluntate omnem a patre consecutum potestatem, quomodo possum de fide destruere monarchiam, quam a patre filio traditam in filio seruo?
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: But as for me, who derive the Son from no other source but from the substance of the Father, and (represent Him) as doing nothing without the Father's will, and as having received all power from the Father, how can I be possibly destroying the Monarchy from the faith, when I preserve it in the Son just as it was committed to Him by the Father?
page: CSEL 47 p. 232 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Son is derived from the Father's substance, does nothing without the Father's will, and received all power from the Father; the monarchy is kept in the Son.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: 'de substantia patris' is the derivation (derivatio) of the Son; answer to objection that the Son destroys the monarchy.
limits: Subordinationists quote 'nihil facientem sine patris uoluntate' and 'consecutum potestatem' as proof of the Son's inferiority. Tertullian's 'derivatio' is origin, not a statement of Nicene equality.

latin: hoc mihi et in tertium gradum dictum sit, quia spiritum non aliunde deputo quam a patre per filium. uide ergo, ne tu potius monarchiam destruas, qui dispositionem et dispensationem eius euertis in tot nominibus constitutam, in quot deus uoluit.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: The same remark (I wish also to be formally) made by me with respect to the third degree in the Godhead, because I believe the Spirit to proceed from no other source than from the Father through the Son. Look to it then, that it be not you rather who are destroying the Monarchy, when you overthrow the arrangement and dispensation of it, which has been constituted in just as many names as it has pleased God to employ.
page: CSEL 47 p. 232 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: The Spirit comes from the Father through the Son (third degree in the Godhead); the 'dispensation' is constituted in as many names as God chose.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Spirit from the Father 'per filium'); useful for the Filioque debate in one direction.
limits: Kroymann emends 'puto' (PMF) to 'deputo' (apparatus: 'deputo scripsi: puto PMF'); the manuscripts read 'puto'. The ANF reads 'believe'. 'Per filium' is the text as printed; it is not the later Filioque formula.

latin: adeo autem manet in suo statu, licet trinitas inferatur, ut etiam restitui habeat patri a filio, siquidem apostolus scribit de ultimo fine: cum tradiderit regnum deo et patri.
latin_edition: Kroymann, CSEL 47 (1906), digital copy on archive.org (quintiseptimiflo47tertuoft). Read from the OCR text layer (djvu.txt) and checked against the rendered scan images of the PDF pages named. Editorial supplements are kept as printed (< > supplied, [ ] secluded by the editor).
english: But it remains so firm and stable in its own state, notwithstanding the introduction into it of the Trinity, that the Son actually has to restore it entire to the Father; even as the apostle says in his epistle, concerning the very end of all: When He shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father;
page: CSEL 47 p. 232 (Latin); ANF vol. 3 page unknown (New Advent page has no print pagination)
edition: Kroymann CSEL 47 (1906) for Latin; ANF vol. 3 (1885) for English
what_it_says: Even with the Trinity introduced, the monarchy stays in its own state, and the Son will hand it back to the Father, citing 1 Cor 15:24.
use: explanation of hard passage: uses 1 Cor 15:24-28 for the Son's eschatological subjection, with the Son's economy and the Father's ultimate unity.
limits: Subordinationists read 'restitui habeat patri a filio' as proof that the Son's rule is lesser and temporary. Tertullian's argument is about the economy, not an eternal hierarchy; the reading is contested.
